title: When ChatGPT joins the team: a mixed-methods study of AI-mediated collaborative lesson design
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether and how ChatGPT changes collaborative lesson-design work when it is positioned as a peer-like feedback provider rather than as a traditional tutor or external tool. The authors focus on a gap in AI-in-education research: much of the literature studies individual use, while less is known about LLMs functioning as active contributors in group learning processes and how that affects both collaboration and learning.

The intervention was a quasi-experimental, counterbalanced crossover study in which 102 in-service teachers in a one-year specialization program for special education completed two authentic group tasks in a single 240-minute session. In one task sequence, groups used ChatGPT 3.5 as a collaborative “team member” to help select and justify inclusive ICT tools and then to design a full lesson/intervention; in the other sequence they completed the same kinds of tasks without ChatGPT. The study combined individual multiple-choice knowledge tests, expert ratings of group-produced artifacts, and written group reflections, allowing the authors to compare learning gains, product quality, and collaborative processes across AI-assisted and non-AI phases.

The main findings suggest that ChatGPT support improved knowledge scores, especially on technology-related content, and that gains made during AI-assisted phases were not immediately lost when the AI was withdrawn. The authors describe this as a Post-Withdrawal Sustained Performance pattern, with stable performance after AI removal within the study window. ChatGPT also appeared to increase efficiency and help groups generate more technology-focused insights, but qualitative evidence showed trade-offs, including reduced peer-to-peer idea building in some groups and concerns about creativity. Overall, the paper argues that LLMs can support collaborative design when learners are scaffolded to critically evaluate AI output rather than accept it passively, but that designers should preserve opportunities for authentic peer dialogue.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based conversational AI chatbot used for text generation, feedback, and general assistance.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a peer-like feedback provider / collaborative team member during group lesson-design tasks; groups were instructed to treat ChatGPT as if it were a colleague and to use it for suggestions, clarification, and critique while designing lesson plans.

findings.finding_summary: In this mixed-methods quasi-experimental study with 102 preservice teachers in 21 groups (82 completed all tests and were included in final analyses), use of ChatGPT was associated with significant gains on the individual knowledge test when it was present in a task phase. For GT1, scores increased after Task 1 (p=0.015, rrb=-0.429) and technology knowledge increased more strongly (p=0.001, rrb=-0.692); for GT2, scores increased when ChatGPT was used in Task 2 (p=0.023, rrb=-0.371; technology subscore p=0.022, rrb=-0.442).
findings.measure: 13-item multiple-choice knowledge test (overall score and technology/methodology subscores)
findings.confidence_interval: GT1 overall: (-0.80, -0.06); GT1 technology: (-1.12, -0.26); GT2 overall: (-0.73, -0.01); GT2 technology: (-0.87, -0.02)
findings.sample_size: n=82 final analysis; GT1 n=38; GT2 n=45

findings.finding_summary: ChatGPT support did not produce a detectable decline after withdrawal in the immediate next phase, indicating a post-withdrawal sustained performance pattern within the study timeframe. For GT1, knowledge remained essentially stable from T1 to T2 (overall p=0.451, rrb=-0.028), and task product quality also did not decline after AI removal (two-sided p=0.236; one-tailed test for decrease p=0.882; d=0.43).
findings.measure: Post-withdrawal knowledge test scores and group artifact quality after AI removal
findings.sample_size: n=38 for GT1 sequence; n=82 final analysis

quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods quasi-experimental study with counterbalanced crossover assignment, but not a randomized controlled trial. It provides quantitative outcome data plus qualitative process evidence, so the methodological strength is moderate rather than high.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported effects on knowledge gains during AI-supported phases are statistically significant and in the modest-to-medium range (e.g., rrb about 0.37 to 0.69 in absolute value), while post-withdrawal performance is maintained rather than further improved. Overall impact is positive but not uniformly large across outcomes.
